Cause Number: 22-036W

Judge: Aaron Bonar
Petitioner
Counsel:

FINDINGS
OF FACT AND CONCLUSIONS OF LAW WITH FINAL ORDER
FINAL ORDER
1.
The
riparian rights boundary between Billington and Adams is determined by IB 56 s Second
Principle, which states that riparian zones are determined by extending the
onshore property boundaries into the public waters in a straight line.
2.
Billington s
boatlift intrudes on Adams riparian zone as it crosses over the boundary
marked by the concrete marker at the southeast corner of Lot 92 as described in
Exhibit 16.
3.
Both
parties are ordered to maintain a clear space of no less than ten (10) feet on
their respective sides of the riparian line. This will create the recommended twenty
(20) feet of clear buffer space between any docks, boatlifts, or other lakeward
structures maintained by either party.
4.
Any
lakeward structures currently maintained and placed by either party must be
moved to comply with this order. Any planned new or expanded lakeward
structures pursued by either party must be planned and constructed in
compliance with this order.
Procedural
Background and Jurisdiction
1.
On
May 5, 2022, Richard Adams (hereinafter Adams) filed correspondence
(hereinafter Petition) with the Natural Resources Commission (hereinafter
Commission) alleging that Matthew Billington (hereinafter Billington), had
placed a boatlift in such a way that it violated Adams riparian rights. See
Petition.
2.
Adams
seeks to have Billington s boatlift moved from Billington s property line
further into Billington s riparian zone, thus allowing Adams to fully use and
enjoy Adams riparian zone and extend Adams dock in accordance with the safety
guidelines outlined in Information Bulletin 56, Riparian Zones within Public
Freshwater Lakes and Navigable Waters, Third Amendment, DIN:
20220209-IR-312220025NRA (hereinafter IB 56). Id at 2.
3.
By
filing his Petition, Adams initiated a proceeding governed by Indiana Code
4-21.5-3, sometimes referred to as the Administrative Orders and Procedures Act
(AOPA) and the administrative rules adopted by the Commission at 312 IAC 3-1 to
assist with the implementation of AOPA. See IC 4-21.5-3-1, et seq.
4.
Administrative
Law Judge (ALJ) Aaron Bonar was appointed under IC 14-10-2-2 to conduct this
proceeding and was assigned this case on May 5, 2022.
5.
A
telephonic prehearing conference was set for May 24, 2022. Following notice to
the parties, the parties attended the prehearing conference as scheduled and
agreed that a settlement could not be reached. Both parties requested that a
hearing be set.
6.
An
administrative hearing took place as scheduled on August 3, 2022. At the
hearing, Adams, Lisa Adams, and Billington appeared in person at the Commission
Hearing Room at the Indiana Government Center in Indianapolis, Indiana. Both
parties appeared pro se .
7.
The
following witnesses provided testimony at the administrative hearing: Richard Adams,
Lisa Adams, and Matthew Billington.
8.
Adams
Exhibits A-J and L-P were offered for admission into the record at the
administrative hearing. Exhibits A-G and M-O were admitted without objection.
Exhibits H-J were admitted over Billington s objections. Exhibit L was
withdrawn.
9.
Billington s
Exhibits 1-6, 8, and 12-17 were offered for admission into the record at the
administrative hearing. Exhibits 6, 8, and 15-17 were admitted without
objection. Exhibits 1-4, 12, 13, and 14 were admitted over Adams objections.
Exhibit 5 was excluded.
10.
The
State of Indiana, through the Department, has been vested by the Indiana
Legislature with full power over public freshwater lakes in the state through
the Lake Preservation Act. IC 14-26-2-5(d).
11.
The
Commission has adopted rules found at 312 IAC 11-3 to assist with the
administration of the Lake Preservation Act. IC 4-21.5-1-15 and 312 IAC
3-1-2.
12.
The
Commission is the ultimate authority of the Department. IC 14-10-2-3.
13.
The
Commission has jurisdiction over the subject matter and the persons in this
dispute.
Findings
of Fact [1]
1.
Richard
Adams and Lisa Adams (hereinafter collectively Adams) purchased property along the
shore of Lake James, a public freshwater lake, in Steuben County, Indiana on or
around April 30, 2021. See Testimony of Richard Adams, Lisa Adams, and Exhibit
13.
2.
The
Adams property is identified as Lot 91 in the plat of Lone Tree Point on Lake
James as recorded in Plat Book 2, page 14 in the Steuben County Recorder s
Office. See Exhibit 13.
3.
Billington
owns property reflected in numerous surveys as Lots 92 and 93 of Lone Tree
Point. Billington owned those lots and lived there with his family prior to
Adams purchasing their property. See testimony of Matthew Billington and
Exhibits 15-16.
4.
Billington s
Lot 92 is bordered by Adams Lot 91. See testimony of Matthew Billington,
Richard Adams, Lisa Adams, Exhibit A, and Exhibits 15-16.
5.
In
the Spring of 2021, Adams hired a local dock services company to assist in
planning an extension of Adams dock in Billington s direction. Adams contends
that the company informed Adams that Billington s boatlift was over Adams
property line and thus interfered with Adams ability to enjoy his riparian
rights. See testimony of Richard Adams.
6.
Adams
contacted Billington shortly afterward regarding the boatlift s placement and
requested that Billington move his boatlift to comply with IB 56, which
suggests at least five (5) feet, but ideally ten (10) feet, of clear space
between Adams dock and Billington s boatlift. [2]
See testimony of Richard Adams, Lisa Adams, and Exhibit B.
7.
Discussions
between the parties continued until at least April 19, 2022, when Billington
informed Adams that he would not discuss the matter any further and reiterated
his belief that his boatlift was not properly placed. Billington s testimony at
the administrative hearing suggested that there was a history of Adams making
frivolous claims against Billington regarding other riparian and property
matters, and that he believed this accusation was also unfounded. See testimony
of Richard Adams, Lisa Adams, and Matthew Billington; see Exhibit I and Exhibit
1.
8.
The
parties dispute the location of the property line between Lots 91 and 92, and
thus the borders of the riparian rights zones granted to both parties. See
totality of the record.
9.
At
the administrative hearing, both parties provided numerous surveys and
photographs of the land and riparian areas in question. The ALJ finds the photographs,
as well as the video submitted by Billington admitted into the record,
illustrative but not conclusive regarding the boundaries of the parties
respective riparian zones. See Exhibits C-E, G, H, J, and M; and Exhibits 2-4,
6, and 8.
10. The
surveys admitted during the hearing, however, provide a firmer third-party
assessment of the properties in question and are more reliable in determining
the dimensions of the riparian zones granted to both parties. The surveys were
conducted by professional surveyors using appropriate technology and
techniques, though both parties testified that surveying techniques, and thus
the surveys resulting from those techniques, may change over time. See testimony
of Richard Adams, Lisa Adams, and Matthew Billingotn; Petitioner s Exhibits A,
F, and N-O; and Respondent s Exhibits 15 and 16.
11. Based
upon the surveys submitted by both parties, the ALJ makes the following
findings:
a. The
combined lake frontage of Billington s Lots 92 and 93 is no more than 96.4
feet. This is illustrated by the measured distance of 46.4 feet of frontage for
Lot 93 and the platted (but not measured) distance of 50 feet of frontage for
Lot 92. On the survey, P and M are used to note platted and measured
distances, respectively. See Exhibit 15.
b. The
lake frontage of Adams Lot 91 is likely between 46 feet and 50 feet. Lot 91 is
platted as having 50 feet of frontage, but neighboring lot 90 is shown to have
49.5 feet of frontage. It is not unreasonable to assume that Adams platted
distance may be a few feet or so different from any measured distance. No
measured distance for Lot 91 was submitted by either party. See Exhibit A and Exhibit
15.
c. The
southeast side of Lot 92, which borders Adams lot, was established by 2 concrete
monuments with 3/8 rods in the center, these monuments were within 0.5 of the
Plat distances to Burlage capped pins found on the SE line of Lot 90. See Exhibit
16.
d. An
October 21, 1993 survey of the same properties by Rowland and Associates was used
as a reference for the survey recorded as Exhibit 15. The Rowland survey was
submitted by Adams as Exhibit F. See Exhibit 16 and Exhibit F. [3]
12. Based
upon the same surveys and IB 56, the ALJ finds that the shoreline shared by
Lots 91 and 92 is not irregular and is roughly a straight line. The ALJ finds
that the lots shown in the surveys intersect the shoreline at roughly
perpendicular angles. Thus, per IB 56 s Second Principle, [w]here the shore
approximates a straight line, and where the onshore property boundaries are
approximately perpendicular to this line, the boundaries of riparian zones are
determined by extending the onshore boundaries into the public waters. See
Exhibit B and illustrations below.
Exhibit
15.
IB
56.
13. At
the administrative hearing, Billington reiterated that his boatlift was placed
within his riparian zone. In the alternative, Billington claimed adverse
possession of any riparian zone of Adams occupied by Billington s boatlift.
See testimony of Matthew Billington.
14. In
addition, Billington testified that his property s prior owners had their
boatlift in the same place, that no complaints had arisen in the past regarding
Billington s boatlift, and that the deed conveying Lot 91 to Adams entitles
Billington to leave his boatlift in place as Adams must take on encumbrances
use and occupancy restrictions easements, rights-of-way, covenants, and
conditions of record with their purchase of Lot 91. See testimony of Matthew
Billington and Exhibits 12-13.
15. Billington s
arguments above are legally unenforceable for the reasons discussed below under
Conclusions of Law. See Conclusions of Law, paragraphs 11-15.
16. Billington
testified that the slight inaccuracies with the surveys submitted could cause
the waterfront measurements to be incorrect, so much so that the boatlift in
question may be within his riparian zone or within Adams riparian zone based
upon the two reference points used when drawing a straight line to define each
party s landward property zones. See testimony of Matthew Billington.
17. The
ALJ is unable to make a finding on this argument as it is outside of his
jurisdiction. See Conclusions of Law, paragraphs 4-5.
Conclusions
of Law
1.
The
Commission is authorized under Indiana Code (IC) 14-10-2 and Indiana
Administrative Code 312 IAC 3-1 to appoint administrative law judges and hold
hearings to resolve disputes surrounding Indiana s natural resources. See IC 14-10-2
and 312 IAC 3-1.
2.
IB
61 identifies Lake James as a public freshwater lake. The State of Indiana has
sole jurisdiction over public freshwater lakes and holds them in the public
trust for Indiana s citizens. See IB 61 (Exhibit P) and IC 14-26-2-5.
3.
The
Commission has jurisdiction over this matter as it concerns the usage of a
public freshwater lake. This proceeding is jurisdictionally appropriate under
IC 4-21.5 and 312 IAC 3-1.
4.
The
Commission s jurisdiction is limited by statutory authority, meaning that the
Commission can only determine matters explicitly granted to it under the
Indiana Code. See Krantz v. Meyers Subdivision Prop. Owners
Ass n , 969 N.E. 2d 1068 (Ind. Ct. App. 2012).
5.
Similarly,
the ALJ is prohibited from making findings regarding the potential changes in
landward property zones. Rather, the ALJ is allowed to review submitted
documents, such as surveys and deeds, to determine rights contained within
those documents to the extent necessary to determine the dimensions and usage
of a riparian zone. See Bowman v. Walls , 14 CADDNAR 85 (2016).
6.
A
pier or boatlift placed by a riparian owner in a public freshwater lake must be
placed in a way that allows for reasonable usage of the lake by all other
riparian owners/users. See Rehlander v. Lenzens, et.al. & Amelio , 15
CADDNAR 115 (2020).
7.
Ideally,
there should be a buffer zone of at least ten (10) feet on both sides of a
dividing line between riparian zones for a total of twenty (20) feet. See IB 56
(Exhibit B) and Rehlander , 15 CADDNAR 115. The buffer zone should be
completely clear of piers, boatlifts, and moored boats.
8.
The
parties riparian zones and rights are determined as described above in
Findings of Fact paragraph 12. As the ALJ is prohibited from assessing landward
property lines and rights, the ALJ concludes that the concrete marker clearly
visible in Adams Exhibit H and Billington s Exhibit 8 is the best demarcation
for the parties respective landward property rights. See Exhibit H and Exhibit
8.
9.
Per
IB 56 and the ALJ s finding that the shoreline along the properties is regular,
the parties riparian zones are established by extending a straight line from
that concrete marker following the property lines as demarcated by the parties
respectively submitted surveys. See IB 56 (Exhibit B), Exhibit A, and Exhibit
15.
10. It
is clear, as shown in Exhibit H and Exhibit 8, that Billington s boatlift is
encroaching on Adams riparian zone. While it is difficult to determine from
the submitted photographs, the boatlift is likely at least a foot over Adams
riparian rights zone. See Exhibit H and Exhibit 8.
11. Billington
raised the issue of adverse possession during the administrative hearing. The
ALJ concludes that Billington s adverse possession argument is not persuasive. The
State of Indiana has sole jurisdiction over the public freshwater lake and
grants property owners along the lake s edge the right to use riparian zones.
Adverse possession thus cannot apply in this matter as Billington cannot claim
adverse possession against the State s granted usage rights.
12. Billington s
argument concerning adverse possession, as stated in his testimony, is more
akin to a prescriptive easement argument. Billington asserted that previous
owners had not raised any issues regarding Billington s boatlift and that he
had always used the dispute area. As discussed in the following paragraphs, no
such easement was ever recorded, rendering this argument moot.
13. Billington s
argument concerning the warranty deeds (Exhibits 12 and 13) requirement to
maintain previous covenants and encumbrances is not persuasive. Exhibit 12, the
deed granting Lot 91 to Michael Redman, Jr., clearly states that the deed is
subject to liens, encumbrances, usage restrictions, easements, rights-of-way,
covenants, and other conditions of record. Exhibit 13, the deed granting the
property from Michael Redman, Jr. to Adams, makes a similar statement. See
Exhibits 12 and 13.
14. Additionally,
Exhibit 13 limits any applicable covenants and warranties to those made by
Redman and states that Grantor [Redman] makes no covenants or warranties as to
the acts of any other person or entity or as to the period prior to its
ownership of the foregoing described real estate. See Exhibit 13.
15. No
evidence was provided to show that any record related to an encumbrance,
easement, or any other act of record granting Billington the right to use the
disputed section of Adams riparian zone. Therefore, Billington may not rely on
his claims regarding the warranty deeds in question for relief.
16. Specifics
regarding Adams proposed dock extension were not entered into the record. The
ALJ does not have specific information on Adams plans to extend his dock,
including how close the planned extension would come to Billington s
established riparian rights zone.
17. Accordingly,
the ALJ concludes that Billington is infringing on Adams riparian rights as
Billington s boatlift is clearly over the line establishing each party s
riparian zones related to Lots 91 and 92. Adams has the right to the full usage
and enjoyment of his riparian zone subject to the limitations of IB 56.
